chapter_theme: Sustained labour builds the doer, funds the virtue of giving and supports one's kin. Faced with fate, the chapter shifts the question: failure of fortune carries no blame, labour always earns its wage, and persistence can outlast what opposes it.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the excellence of effort (611-613), the fault of lacking it (614), the good of having it (615), effort and its absence as causes of wealth and poverty (616-617), and effort despite fate (618-620).

611.reading: One must not slacken by saying 'this is hard', because effort brings the greatness needed.
611.nuance: Difficulty is measured against a self that labour itself enlarges, so the calculation 'this is too much for me' is wrong in its premise. Parimelazhagar makes this explicit.

612.reading: Guard against letting a task die in the middle of the doing, for the world's bond with a person turns on how they have dealt with the work's unmet need.
612.nuance: A short verse gives opposite readings of தீர்ந்தார்: those who left the work or those who finished it. Parimelazhagar glosses குறை from Purananuru 188, which is a thread beyond the Kural.

positions.position: தீர்ந்தார் are those who abandoned the needed work, and the world abandons them.
positions.quote: வினையாகிய குறையைச் செய்யாது விட்டாரை உலகம் விட்டது

positions.position: தீர்ந்தார் are those who completed it, and the world does not leave them.

613.reading: The proud distinction called helping others stands on the quality called labour.
613.nuance: Manakkudavar draws the implication plainly: even doing virtue comes from this. A moral excellence has an economic foundation, and தாளாண்மை and வேளாண்மை rhyme to tie them.

614.reading: The generosity of one who won't labour comes to nothing, like a sword in the hand of a பேடி.
614.nuance: The image depends on a period contempt for a third-gender person, which commentators extend by saying the figure wishes to fight but is too afraid. Manakkudavar alone drops the word and says 'one who fears at the sight of arms'.

615.reading: One who desires the work and not pleasure is a pillar who wipes away his kin's troubles and bears them up.
615.nuance: Parimelazhagar finds a principle of causes here: wanting the cause rather than the effect gets all effects, and wanting the effect without the cause gets nothing. The pillar stands under others' weight, so personal renunciation of pleasure is here for one's household, not for liberation.

616.reading: Effort builds prosperity, and the absence of effort ushers in the absence of everything.
616.nuance: முயற்றின்மை இன்மை: absence brings absence. The verse's symmetry leaves no room for a third cause, and that is what 371 and 377 dispute.

positions.position: திருவினை means wealth, and specifically a king's six limbs of state.
positions.quote: அரசர்மாட்டு உளதாய முயற்சி அவரது செல்வத்தினை வளர்க்கும்

positions.position: It yields excellent deeds and achievements, not wealth as such.

617.reading: They say the dark goddess of misfortune lives in sloth, and she of the lotus lives in the labour of the unslothful.
617.nuance: என்ப, 'they say', keeps a little distance from the claim: the verse reports it. தாள் can mean both foot and exertion, and so Lakshmi may be at the feet of the one who works.

positions.position: The goddesses are taken as they are, dwelling respectively in sloth and in effort, with sin's blackness assigned to the first.
positions.quote: பாவத்தின் கருமை அதன் பயனாக முகடிமேல் ஏற்றப்பட்டது.

positions.position: The names are mere words used to point at the energetic person and the idler.

618.reading: Lacking good fortune is no one's disgrace; failing to work, after learning what must be known, is the disgrace.
618.nuance: The verse does not say effort defeats fate. It moves the question from causes to blame, and that is a different and more defensible claim than 620's. அறிவறிந்து adds a condition: blind labour isn't what is being asked for.

positions.position: பொறி is fate: people blame present faults, not fruits of past deeds.
positions.quote: உலகம் பழவினை பற்றிப் பழியாது, ஈண்டைக் குற்றமுடைமை பற்றியே பழிப்பது

positions.position: பொறி is religious merit: lacking it is no fault, and this answers those who say effort is useless without merit.
The idea of blame from fate is itself wrong.

619.reading: Though divine order may deny the end sought, effort still pays the wage of the body's strain.
619.nuance: கூலி is a modest word: a labourer's wage, not the prize. The verse concedes the goal may be lost, and secures only a floor.

positions.position: தெய்வம் is fate: where it withholds, one gets a wage, and where it favours, much more. So don't wait on it.
positions.quote: முயன்ற வினை பால்வகையால் கருதிய பயனைத் தாராதாயினும்

positions.position: தெய்வம் stands for merit: without it there's no gain, yet effort pays in proportion to strain.
It refers to God and prayer: what crying out to God won't achieve, labour will.
positions.quote: கடவுளே என்று கூவி அழைப்பதால் நடக்காத காரியம்

620.reading: Those who toil on without flagging or delay will see even fate's back.
620.nuance: உப்பக்கம் காண்பர் is a battle image: to see an enemy's back as it retreats. Pope's rendering, with fate put 'behind their back', turns the image around.

positions.position: Fate can obstruct once or twice but not always, so repeated effort outlasts it.
positions.quote: ஊழ் ஒருகாலாக இருகாலாக அல்லது விலக்கலாகாமையின், பலகால் முயல்வார் பயன் எய்துவர்

positions.position: They actually conquer fate, turning back the bad karma that blocks the fruit.

links.note: 380 asks what could be stronger than fate, which arrives ahead of every stratagem. 620 answers that those who keep toiling see its back. Parimelazhagar narrows the gap by saying fate blocks only a few attempts, which the two verses themselves don't say.

377 limits what even hoarders of millions can enjoy to what has been apportioned. 619 guarantees effort a wage whatever divine order decides. One sets a ceiling on enjoyment and the other a floor on reward, and they may coexist only just.
The same sword in the same hand. In 614 it stands for generosity without labour and in 727 for learning without courage in an assembly. Both say an asset is void without the disposition to use it.

source_issues: 611: Parimelazhagar's commentary is truncated at the start: the gloss of the first line is missing.
617: The verse reads தாளுளான் where Parimelazhagar's gloss has தாள் உளாள், matching the feminine subject. It may be a text variant or an error.
620: Parimelazhagar's word-gloss is almost entirely missing; only the explanation survives.
